title: Word Break II
description: Brute force to optimized: unmemoized recursive segmentation versus memoizing by starting index.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given a string s and a dictionary of words wordDict, return every possible way to segment s into a space separated sequence of one or more dictionary words.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Problem Summary","Return every valid way to split s into consecutive words that all appear in wordDict."],["Input","s, a string of length n, and wordDict, a list of distinct dictionary words."],["Output","A list of sentences, each a space separated sequence of dictionary words that reconstructs s exactly."],["Constraints","1 <= s.length <= 20, 1 <= wordDict.length <= 1000, all dictionary words are distinct."],["Requirements","Every word used in a sentence must come from wordDict, and the words in a sentence, joined together, must reconstruct s exactly."]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Pattern","Recursive segmentation memoized by starting index, so each distinct suffix of s is fully resolved exactly once."],["Difficulty","Advanced"],["Tags","Strings, Dynamic Programming, Recursion and Backtracking"],["Interview Focus","Recognizing that the same starting index can be reached through many different earlier word choices, and memoizing by that single index eliminates all the redundant re-solving."]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a string s and a dictionary of words wordDict, return every possible way to segment s into a space separated sequence of one or more dictionary words.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding Every Way to Split a Run-Together Phrase
blocks.text: Like taking a phrase with all its spaces removed and finding every possible way to reinsert spaces so that each resulting piece is a real, recognized word from a dictionary.

blocks.caption: Every valid way to cut the string into a sequence of dictionary words counts as an answer

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: s = "catsanddog", wordDict = ["cat", "cats", "and", "sand", "dog"]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Segmentation","Sentence","Why"],"rows":[["\"cats\" + \"and\" + \"dog\"","\"cats and dog\"","each piece is a valid dictionary word and together they reconstruct s exactly"],["\"cat\" + \"sand\" + \"dog\"","\"cat sand dog\"","a different split of the same string, also using only dictionary words"]]}

blocks.text: Example: s = "pineapplepenapple", wordDict = ["apple", "pen", "applepen", "pine", "pineapple"]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Segmentation","Sentence","Why"],"rows":[["\"pine\" + \"apple\" + \"pen\" + \"apple\"","\"pine apple pen apple\"","four short dictionary words reconstructing s exactly"],["\"pineapple\" + \"pen\" + \"apple\"","\"pineapple pen apple\"","a longer dictionary word absorbs what was two words in the previous segmentation"],["\"pine\" + \"applepen\" + \"apple\"","\"pine applepen apple\"","yet another valid grouping using a different combined dictionary word"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: s = "catsandog", wordDict = ["cats", "dog", "sand", "and", "cat"]
No combination of dictionary words can be arranged to exactly reconstruct "catsandog", so the answer is an empty list.
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask whether different segmentation paths ever end up needing to solve the exact same remaining problem.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Wildcard Matching and Interleaving String already showed that memoizing by whatever position (or positions) fully determines a subproblem removes redundant recomputation across different recursive paths.

Observation 2: Here, a subproblem depends on just a single number, the starting index, since everything before it has already been fixed by whichever words were chosen so far, simpler than those two-position problems but the same underlying principle.

Observation 3: The exact same starting index can be reached through many different earlier sequences of word choices, so storing the complete list of valid sentences for a starting index the first time it is solved, and simply reusing that list whenever the same index is reached again, avoids ever re-solving the identical suffix.

Observation 4: Tracing s equal to "catsanddog" confirms it, the starting index 7 is reached both through "cats" then "and", and separately through "cat" then "sand", yet its solved sentence list is computed only once and reused by both paths.

Recognizing that many different earlier word choices can converge on the exact same starting index is what justifies memoizing by that index, turning redundant re-solving into a single computation reused everywhere it is needed.
6. Brute Force Solution
Recursively try every dictionary word as a possible prefix match starting at the current position, and recurse on whatever remains after removing that matched word, combining the results.
Step by step algorithm

items: At the current starting position, try every word in the dictionary as a candidate match against the upcoming characters.
If it matches, recursively find every way to segment the remainder of the string.
Combine the matched word with every valid segmentation of the remainder to build complete sentences.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Reaching the end of the string is the base case, representing a single valid, empty continuation for whatever sentence has been built so far.
Every candidate word length starting from the current position is tried, so no valid dictionary word match at this position is ever missed.
Each matched word is combined with every valid completion of the remainder, since a single matching word can lead to multiple different full sentences.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every possible dictionary word match at every position is explored, so every valid segmentation is correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential in the worst case, since the same starting position can be recursed into repeatedly through different earlier word choices.
Space: O(n) for the recursion stack, plus space for the accumulated sentences.
Limitation: the exact same suffix of the string, starting at the exact same index, gets fully resolved over and over again every time a different earlier path happens to land back on that same index.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: many different sequences of earlier word choices can land on the exact same starting index, and each arrival re-derives that suffix's entire sentence list from scratch.

What memoizing by starting index fixes directly: storing a suffix's complete solved sentence list the first time it is computed lets every later arrival at that same index just reuse it.

What memoization cannot avoid: since the number of valid sentences can itself be exponential for some inputs, no technique can make producing an exponential output cheaper than the output itself.

The core idea: keep the exact same recursive structure, but check a memo table by starting index first, and only do the recursive work if that index has never been solved before.

Memoize the recursion by starting index: store the complete list of valid sentences for the suffix starting at each index the first time it is computed, and simply reuse that stored list immediately if the same starting index is ever reached again through a different earlier path. This ensures each distinct suffix is only ever solved once, no matter how many different ways there are to reach it.
9. Optimized Solution
The same recursive structure, but with a memo table keyed by starting index so each suffix is solved exactly once.
Dry run for s = "catsanddog" (partial, showing memoization reuse)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Starting index","Action"],"rows":[["index 10 (end of string)","base case, returns [\"\"]. computed once, reused by every path that reaches it"],["index 7 (\"dog\")","matches \"dog\", combines with the cached result from index 10. computed once, reused by both \"cats and\" and \"cat sand\" paths"],["index 0","tries \"cat\" and \"cats\" as prefixes, combining each with the already solved suffixes"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: memoize by starting index so each distinct suffix is solved exactly once

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because the list of valid sentences for the suffix starting at a given index depends only on that index and the fixed string and dictionary, never on how that index was reached, so storing and reusing the result the first time it is computed is always correct, regardless of which earlier path arrives at it.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["A starting index is reached for the very first time","Its full sentence list is computed recursively and stored in the memo table","Future arrivals at this exact index can skip the recursive work entirely"],["A starting index is reached again through a different earlier path","The memo table returns the previously stored list immediately","No redundant recomputation happens, no matter how many paths converge on this index"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times the total number of valid sentences), since generating and combining the output strings is itself the dominant cost when many segmentations exist, though each distinct suffix's recursive work is only ever done once.
Space: O(n times the total number of valid sentences), for the memo table storing every suffix's full sentence list.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Reuses Prior Work","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Brute force (unmemoized recursion)","Exponential","O(n) recursion stack","No, identical suffixes re-solved repeatedly","Correct, but wastes enormous effort on repeated work."],["Optimized (memoized by starting index)","O(n times total sentences)","O(n times total sentences)","Yes, each suffix solved exactly once","The expected answer, eliminating all redundant recomputation."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Since the number of valid segmentations can itself be exponential for certain inputs (a string made entirely of one repeated letter with a dictionary of all short prefixes of it, for example), memoization removes redundant recomputation of shared subproblems, but it cannot avoid the fundamentally exponential cost of producing an exponential number of distinct sentences when that many genuinely exist.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to memoize entirely, which causes the same suffix to be resolved repeatedly across many different call paths, unnecessarily blowing up the running time.

Not first checking whether s can be segmented at all using a simpler boolean check (the related "Word Break" problem), which can save significant wasted work by immediately returning an empty result for clearly impossible inputs before attempting to build any sentences.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["s that cannot be segmented at all","Should return an empty list rather than attempting a partial or best effort segmentation."],["A dictionary containing many overlapping words of different lengths","Increases the branching factor and the number of valid segmentations significantly."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Mention the optional early pruning step: first run the simpler "can s be segmented at all" boolean check using standard dynamic programming, and only attempt full sentence generation if that check succeeds, since it can quickly rule out entirely impossible inputs.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid re-solving the same suffix", think: memoize by starting index, since a subproblem depends only on that single position.
If the interviewer says "can you rule out impossible inputs faster", think: run the simpler boolean Word Break check first, before attempting to generate any sentences.
If the interviewer says "why can't this run in polynomial time in general", think: the number of valid sentences can itself be exponential, so producing them all can never be faster than the output size.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why does memoizing by starting index alone, rather than by some other combination of state, correctly capture every subproblem?
How would you first check whether s can be segmented at all, without generating any actual sentences?
How would you return just the count of valid segmentations, without materializing every sentence?
How would this approach change if dictionary words could repeat or overlap heavily with each other?
How would you adapt this approach to segment s using the fewest possible number of words?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Wildcard Matching and Interleaving String, whose 2D memoization by a pair of positions is the same principle applied here to a single position instead.

Palindrome Partitioning, whose backtracking enumeration also has an inherently exponential output size, where the goal is eliminating redundant recomputation rather than beating the output size itself.

Any recursive enumeration problem where the same subproblem, identified by a small piece of state like a single index, can be reached through many different paths, where memoizing by that state removes all redundant work.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: exponential time, O(n) recursion stack space (not counting accumulated sentence storage). Optimized (memoized by starting index): time and space proportional to n times the total number of valid sentences, avoiding redundant recomputation of any shared suffix.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: recursive segmentation memoized by starting index, so each distinct suffix of s is fully resolved exactly once.

Core Idea: the same starting index can be reached through many different earlier word choices, so storing and reusing each index's solved sentence list the first time it is computed eliminates all redundant re-solving.
Time: exponential for the brute force, O(n times total sentences) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) recursion stack for the brute force, O(n times total sentences) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: memoization removes redundant recomputation, but it cannot make an inherently exponential output any smaller, since every valid sentence genuinely must be produced.
Interview Difficulty: the memoization itself is simple once recognized; explaining why the output size, not the algorithm, is the true complexity bottleneck is what shows real depth.
One line memory trick: memoize every suffix's solved sentence list by its starting index, and reuse it the moment any path reaches that same index again.
